questions.def: Each takes a singular verb, even with a plural noun after 'of'.
questions.question: Each of the students ___ a pencil.

questions.def: When using 'neither/nor,' the verb agrees with the closest noun.
questions.question: Neither the cat nor the dogs ___ outside.

questions.def: Nouns ending in -ics often take a singular verb (politics).
questions.question: Politics ___ a difficult subject.

questions.def: 'A lot of' takes a plural verb when referring to people.
questions.question: A lot of people ___ to the party.

questions.def: Family can be singular (as a unit) or plural.
questions.question: My family ___ happy with the decision.

questions.def: 'Everyone' is singular and takes a singular verb (is).
questions.question: Everyone are invited to the party.

questions.def: 'There are' agrees with the plural noun 'reasons'.
questions.question: There ___ many reasons to go.

questions.def: With uncountable nouns, 'some of' takes a singular verb.
questions.question: Some of the cake ___ gone.

questions.def: Team can be singular (as a unit) or plural. 'is' is more common.
questions.question: The team ___ playing well today.

questions.def: 'All that he needs' functions as a singular subject.
questions.question: All that he ___ is love.

questions.def: Money is uncountable, so 'most of' takes a singular verb.
questions.question: Most of the money ___ spent.

questions.def: With 'neither/nor', verb agrees with the closest subject (I).
questions.question: Neither she nor I ___ going to the party.

questions.def: 'News' is singular, even though it looks plural.
questions.question: The news ___ surprising.

questions.def: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and verb.
questions.question: Many a student ___ late.

questions.def: Physics is a singular subject, despite the 's'.
questions.question: Physics ___ my favorite subject.

questions.def: Committee can be singular or plural, but 'its' suggests singular.
questions.question: The committee ___ made its decision.

questions.def: None can be singular or plural, but 'food' is uncountable, so singular.
questions.question: None of the food ___ left.

questions.def: With 'either/or', the verb agrees with the closest subject (Mary).
questions.question: Either John or Mary ___ going to help.

questions.def: Staff is plural and refers to a group of people.
questions.question: The staff ___ working hard.

questions.def: 'The majority of' takes a plural verb when referring to people.
questions.question: The majority of students ___ present.

questions.def: Since there are multiple items, use the plural 'are'.
questions.question: There ___ a book and some pens on the desk.

questions.def: Nobody is singular and needs the singular verb 'knows'.
questions.question: Nobody know the answer to the question.

questions.def: 'Measles' is singular, even though it ends in 's'.
questions.question: Measles ___ a contagious disease.

questions.def: 'A pair of' is singular and requires a singular verb.
questions.question: A pair of shoes ___ on the floor.

questions.def: One person is both your friend and colleague, so use singular verb.
questions.question: My friend and colleague ___ arriving soon.

questions.def: Each/every takes a singular verb, even with a plural noun nearby.
questions.question: Each of the students ___ a book.

questions.def: With 'neither/nor', the verb agrees with the *closest* noun.
questions.question: Neither John nor Mary ___ to the party.

questions.def: News is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
questions.question: The news ___ very surprising.

questions.def: 'A lot of' followed by a plural noun takes a plural verb.
questions.question: A lot of people ___ happy about the news.

questions.def: Some nouns ending in -s (like politics) are singular.
questions.question: Politics ___ a difficult subject.
